title: Subject-matter and objectives
text: Establishes GDPR scope and objectives: protection of natural persons with regard to processing of personal data and free movement of such data.
summary: Sets the scope and aims of the Regulation: protect personal data rights and ensure free flow of data within the EU under common rules.
simple: This article says what the GDPR is for: protecting people's personal data and allowing data to move within the EU under the same rules.
scenarios: A company operating in the EU must follow GDPR when processing personal data.
Processing that occurs wholly outside the EU but targets EU residents may fall under GDPR.

faqs.q: Does Article 1 apply to non-EU companies?
faqs.a: Yes if they offer goods/services to or monitor behavior of people in the EU.

title: Material scope
text: Defines which processing activities are covered by GDPR and lists exceptions (e.g., for activities outside scope like purely personal/household activities).
summary: Specifies what kinds of data processing are subject to the GDPR and outlines limited exceptions.
simple: This explains which data-processing activities the GDPR controls and what it doesn't cover (like strictly personal use).
scenarios: An employer's employee records are covered by GDPR.
A person keeping a personal address book for private use is not covered.

faqs.a: Properly anonymised data are not personal data and fall outside GDPR.

title: Territorial scope
text: Explains when GDPR applies to processing activities carried out in the context of an establishment in the EU, and in some cases to controllers/processors outside the EU.
summary: Explains when processing performed in or targeted at the EU is covered by GDPR, including some extra-territorial situations.
simple: This article says when GDPR applies based on where a company is established or where the people being targeted live.
scenarios: An online service based outside the EU that targets EU customers must comply with GDPR.
A data controller established in the EU is always covered for its processing activities.

faqs.q: Does running an EU-language website mean GDPR applies?
faqs.a: Not automatically; it depends on whether the site targets EU residents (e.g., EU prices, delivery to EU).

title: Definitions
text: Provides key definitions used throughout the GDPR, such as 'personal data', 'processing', 'controller', 'processor', 'consent', etc.
summary: Defines core terms used in the GDPR so readers understand obligations and rights consistently.
simple: This is the glossary: it explains the important words the GDPR uses, like what 'personal data' means.
scenarios: Distinguishing a controller (decides why/what data to process) from a processor (acts on instructions).
Understanding that 'personal data' includes online identifiers like IP addresses in some cases.

faqs.a: Any operation on personal data: collection, storage, use, deletion, etc.

title: Principles relating to processing of personal data
text: Sets principles: lawfulness, fairness, transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability.
summary: Lists the core principles organisations must follow when processing personal data and introduces accountability.
simple: This article gives the 'rules' for good data handling: only collect what's needed, keep it accurate, be transparent, and keep data safe.
scenarios: Collecting only necessary fields during signup (data minimisation).
Keeping a clear retention schedule and deleting data no longer needed (storage limitation).

faqs.a: Only collecting and keeping the personal data needed for the stated purpose.

Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences
Processing that does not require identification
Transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of the rights of the data subject
Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
Information to be provided where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject
Right of access by the data subject
Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten')
Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing
Data protection by design and by default
Representatives of controllers or processors not established in the Union
Processing under the authority of the controller or processor
Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject
